submission.natural_language_explanation: Retrospective and context-free: at layer 0 this pole is a piece lookup, so its strength is a fixed function of the current BPE piece (token identity explains 100% of the scan variance, the preceding tokens contribute nothing, and a piece scores the same alone or in a sentence), and it fires on a fixed union of two lexical clusters - occurrence quantifiers, i.e. frequency adverbs of how often (seldom 0.91, frequently 0.84, rarely 0.74, invariably 0.70, always/usually/never/oftentimes 0.56-0.66, sometimes, occasionally, regularly, typically, infrequently) together with the '-n' stems of negated auxiliaries (isn 0.91, wasn 0.73, wouldn 0.69, hasn 0.53, aren 0.48, shouldn 0.43, doesn 0.32, weren 0.33, hadn, didn, don) and Graeco-Latin technical/biomedical stems and capitalised word-initial fragments (Staphylococcus 0.78, Escherichia 0.69, Salmonella, bacteri-, infect-, microbiome, antibiotics, medications, hepatitis, influenza, amino, acetyl, magnesium 0.55, zinc, and the En-/Ein-/Eisen-/Cros-/Stern- name pieces, e.g. 'En' of Enchant and Enlightenment at 0.78). It is silent on the bare auxiliaries (is, was, are, would), on the word 'not', on certainty and manner adverbs (certainly, definitely, easily, properly), on pathogen words that are not Graeco-Latin stems (virus, disease, coli) and on ordinary everyday nouns (house, food, book, time, people), however close those are in meaning or slot.

Broader reading: it is a general non-core/technical-vocabulary detector that fires on any infrequent, technical-looking or foreign-looking piece, including manner adverbs ('quickly', 'carefully'), ordinary pathogen words ('virus', 'disease') and famous names ('Churchill', 'Darwin'), which this hypothesis predicts stay at or below the 0.25-of-max line.

Biomedical reading (the one the Jacobian lens suggests): the pole is the microbiology/infection feature and fires on ' antibiotics', 'Salmonella' and ' microbiome' because of their meaning, while the frequency adverbs and negated auxiliaries would not fire.

# Clear variables inside Module

I have a function that uses Module. The function takes as input a .csv that can have as many columns as it wishes to, and it will import all of them. The user just needs to call function[num], and it will import num columns of the .csv. This of course is a oversimplified version of the idea of my code. To accomplish the "unknown" number of variables I used MapThread like the following.

f[num_]:=Module[{colorlist, cnamelist},
colorlist = {};
For[i = 0, i < num, i++,
AppendTo[colorlist,
Directive[Opacity[1],
Defer[RGBColor] @@@ ColorData["Rainbow", 1 - i/(num - 1)]]]];
cnamelist = {};
For[i = 1, i <= num, i++,
AppendTo[cnamelist, StringJoin["c", ToString[i]]]];


If num is set to 7, then it creates a list colorlist={"c1", "c2" ... "c7"} and then defines the variables c1, c2... c7 with a corresponding color through MapThread.

Everything works, the issue is that c1,c2, ... c7 are now defined and I cant use MapThread again. Since its inside a function the purpose it to use it again.

I tried adding to the function in the last line the following bit

For[i = 1, i <= num, i++, Clear[cnamelist[[i]] ] ]


But it returns the error Clear::ssym: cnamelist[[i]] is not a symbol or a string.

How can I clear all the variables. I have more lists like cnamelist in my code that needs to be cleared for it to work again, but I would assume the same procedure would work.

• Use Clear[cnamelist] or Delete[cnamelist , i], if you want to delete single elements from the list (note that the list gets shorter so that enumeration changes). – Henrik Schumacher Jun 13 '18 at 17:38
• Clear[cnamelist] clears cnamelist but not the variables c1,c2, ...c7 that are inside it. Tried putting Delete[cnamelist , i] instead of Clear[cnamelist[[i]] ] in the For but nothing changed, they dont clear. – M.O. Jun 13 '18 at 17:42
• Btw.: Try to avoid AppendTo. Usually it involves copying the whole list. Just compare these timings: a = {}; Do[AppendTo[a, i], {i, 100000}]; // AbsoluteTiming b = Range[1000000]; // AbsoluteTiming – Henrik Schumacher Jun 13 '18 at 17:50
• Are there any good reasons why you want that function to define variables as a side effect instead of just returning the column data? While Mathematica does allow you to do that, it is a very unusual behavior for a function and I would consider it in almost all cases a bad idea that will almost certainly cause problems at some point. Why don't you just return the data as an array? – Albert Retey Jun 13 '18 at 22:51
• I am not sure I understood your question. The example here is like that because I followed the same procedure than a previous portion of the code. The function imports data to be plotted from a .csv. The bit here is the color portion of the plots which copies the structure (code wise) of the part that imports the data. Viral myocarditis mimicking acute myocardial infarction.
Anecdotal reports have shown that myocarditis can mimic acute myocardial infarction with chest pain, electrocardiographic (ECG) abnormalities, serum creatine kinase elevation and hemodynamic instability. Thirty-four patients with clinical signs and symptoms consistent with acute myocardial infarction underwent right ventricular endomyocardial biopsy during a 6.5-year period after angiographic identification of normal coronary anatomy. Myocarditis was found on histologic study in 11 of these 34 patients. Cardiogenic shock requiring intraaortic balloon support developed within 6 h of admission in three (27%) of the patients with myocarditis. The mean age of the group with myocarditis was 42 +/- 5 years. A preceding viral illness had been present in six patients (54%). The ECG abnormalities were varied and included ST segment elevation (n = 6), T wave inversions (n = 3), ST segment depression (n = 2) and pathologic Q waves (n = 2). The ECG abnormalities were typically seen in the anterior precordial leads but were diffusely evident in three patients. Left ventricular function was normal in six patients and globally decreased in the remaining five patients, whose ejection fraction ranged from 14% to 45%. Lymphocytic myocarditis was diagnosed in 10 patients, and giant cell myocarditis was detected in the remaining patient. Four patients with impaired left ventricular function received immunosuppressive therapy with prednisone and either azathioprine (n = 2) or cyclosporine (n = 2). All six patients whose left ventricular function was normal on admission remain alive in functional class I. Of the five patients with impaired systolic function, ejection fraction normalized in three of the four patients who received immunosuppressive therapy within 3 months of treatment and in the one patient who received only supportive therapy.(ABSTRACT TRUNCATED AT 250 WORDS)

adversarial_test_results.detail: Bare 'was', 'were' and 'would' with 'not' and ordinary nouns: the near-miss auxiliaries lack the claimed '-n' stems.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: He certainly tried, and he finished the job easily and properly, though anyone who says it went definitely well is exaggerating a little.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Certainty and manner adverbs (certainly, definitely, easily, properly) are named as silent, while the broader technical-vocabulary rival predicts firing here.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The virus spread through the school, and the disease closed the market for a week after a single coli outbreak in the canteen.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Pathogen words that are not Graeco-Latin stems (virus, disease, coli) are named as silent, while the broader and biomedical rivals predict them active.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The food in the house was fine, and the book on the table had a picture of the time before people moved to this street.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Ordinary everyday nouns only; the hypothesis names food, house, book, time and people as silent, so no piece should fire.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: She is not going to the meeting, was not told about it, and would not care either way about the result.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Bare auxiliaries and the word 'not' without any '-n' clause stem; every reading, including the narrower one, predicts silence.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The frequent delays made the usual trip slow, and the rare stops were a regular nuisance for everyone on the platform.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Adjectival frequent, usual, rare and regular are different pieces from the claimed -ly adverbs, so piece lookup predicts silence.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The frequency of the signal was measured twice, and the rate of change mattered more than the total number of pulses.
adversarial_test_results.detail: The noun 'frequency' is a different piece from the claimed adverb 'frequently', so the hypothesis predicts no activation.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The train stopped en route to the coast, and the menu was printed en masse in a dialect that nobody in the village could read.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Lowercase ' en' in French loan phrases is a different piece from the claimed capitalised ' En' name fragments; only the foreign-looking rival predicts firing.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The software logs an error when the keyboard stops responding, and the screen stays blank until someone restarts the machine.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Native-English technical vocabulary (software, keyboard) with no claimed Graeco-Latin stem; the broader technical-vocabulary rival predicts firing and the hypothesis does not.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The ward was quiet; nurses checked the patients every hour and wrote the symptoms on a chart by the bed.
adversarial_test_results.detail: A clinical infection setting with no claimed Graeco-Latin stem; the biomedical rival should fire on the topic while the hypothesis stays silent.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: La casa no es fría en invierno, y la comida está buena; la gente del libro habla de la época en que vivían aquí.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Spanish keeps the domestic topic and the 'is not' meaning but uses other pieces, so the hypothesis predicts silence and only the foreign-looking rival predicts firing.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Das Haus ist kalt und das Essen ist gut, aber die Leute im Buch sagen, dass es nicht stimmt.
adversarial_test_results.detail: German uses 'ist' and 'nicht' rather than the English ' isn' or ' not' pieces, so token lookup predicts silence while the foreign-looking rival predicts firing.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Would you please open the window, and could you close the book on the table before the people arrive for dinner?
adversarial_test_results.detail: Bare 'Would' and 'could' as sentence-initial requests, named as silent auxiliaries, with ordinary nouns throughout.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: They are reading the book about time, and the people in the house are cooking food for the guests tonight.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Bare 'are' plus the ordinary nouns book, time, people, house and food, all named as silent by the hypothesis.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: You cannot enter the house without a key, and the food in the kitchen cannot be moved before noon on Sunday.
adversarial_test_results.detail: The fused 'cannot' is one piece rather than the claimed ' not' or ' don' stems, so the hypothesis predicts silence.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: An occasional visitor finds the typical layout odd, and the usual seats near the door are taken by noon.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Adjectival occasional, typical and usual are different pieces from the claimed adverbs occasionally, typically and usually, so the hypothesis predicts silence.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: She quickly packed the bag and carefully checked the tickets, then walked slowly to the platform where the train waited.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Manner adverbs quickly, carefully and slowly are named as silent; the broader technical-vocabulary rival is the reading that predicts firing.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Churchill and Darwin are both remembered in the museum, and the guide tells a story about each of them at the entrance.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Famous names whose pieces are not in the claimed En-/Ein-/Eisen-/Cros-/Stern- list, so the hypothesis predicts silence while the broader names rival predicts firing.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The English edition came out first, and the editors added a short preface for readers in other markets.
adversarial_test_results.detail: The word 'English' surfaces as the single token ' English', not the claimed ' En' fragment, so the hypothesis predicts silence here.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: She always arrives before the coffee is ready, and he never leaves the office before the cleaners finish their rounds.
adversarial_test_results.detail: ' always' and ' never' are claimed frequency adverbs absent from the top examples; the narrower and biomedical rivals predict silence.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The old ferry seldom runs in winter, and the villagers seldom complain about the delay in the harbour.
adversarial_test_results.detail: ' seldom' is the highest-scoring claimed frequency adverb, shown here in a novel maritime context; only the hypothesis and the broader rival predict firing.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The market rarely calms this quickly, and the traders invariably blame the weather for the sudden drop in prices.
adversarial_test_results.detail: ' rarely' and ' invariably' are claimed frequency adverbs in a finance context unlike the examples; the narrower and biomedical rivals predict silence.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The bond isn't yielding what it did last year, and the fund isn't paying out on schedule this quarter.
adversarial_test_results.detail: The claimed ' isn' piece (tokenised as ' isn' + "'t") in a financial context unlike the examples; the biomedical rival predicts silence while the hypothesis and narrower rival predict firing.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Health inspectors found Salmonella in the batch of eggs, so the shop recalled each carton it had sold that morning.
adversarial_test_results.detail: ' Salmonella' is a named Graeco-Latin biomedical stem (tokenised here as ' Sal' + 'monella') in a food-safety context; the narrower negated-auxiliary rival predicts silence.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The culture grew Escherichia coli overnight, and the lab reported the finding to the clinic the next day.
adversarial_test_results.detail: ' Escherichia' is named as an activating Graeco-Latin stem but surfaces here as a single token rather than the claimed 'herichia' piece, so this tests the hypothesis's word-level claim; the narrower negated-auxiliary rival predicts silence.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The supplement label lists magnesium and zinc, along with a small dose of vitamin B6 and fish oil.
adversarial_test_results.detail: ' magnesium' and ' zinc' are claimed Graeco-Latin stems but not infection words, so the hypothesis and broader rival predict firing while the microbiology rival should not.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: My grandfather met Einstein once in 1935, and Eisenhower came through the same town a few years later.
adversarial_test_results.detail: ' Eisenhower' carries the claimed 'Eisen' name piece (while 'Einstein' is a single token) in a biographical context unlike the code example, so the hypothesis predicts firing and the narrower and biomedical rivals do not.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Her first novel, Enchant, sold well in spring, and the sequel came out a year later.
adversarial_test_results.detail: The claimed ' En' fragment of 'Enchant' (tokenised as ' En' + 'chant') appears in running prose rather than inside a code identifier, a context unlike the example, and no rival reading predicts firing.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Each row has two columns, one marked En for English and one marked Fr for French, and the translator fills in both.
adversarial_test_results.detail: A standalone capitalised ' En' token used as an abbreviation rather than a name fragment; the context-free piece-lookup hypothesis predicts firing while the negated-auxiliary and biomedical rivals do not.
